849.trap_explanation: Statement 2 inverts the complaint rule — it says 'only a Member' can complain, but any person can complain (non-members route it through an MP). Students mistake the procedural channel requirement for a substantive eligibility bar.

statements.text: Initially it was an ad-hoc Committee.
statements.reason: Speaker G.M.C. Balayogi constituted it as an ad-hoc committee in 2000. It became a permanent Standing Committee only in August 2015 under Rule 316A.

statements.text: Only a Member of the Lok Sabha can make a complaint relating to unethical conduct of a member of the Lok Sabha.
statements.reason: Any person can file a complaint. Non-members must route it through a Lok Sabha MP and submit an affidavit. The MP is a conduit, not the sole eligible complainant.

statements.text: This Committee cannot take up any matter which is sub-judice.
statements.reason: The Committee explicitly bars sub-judice matters — cases pending before courts are outside its jurisdiction to preserve judicial independence.

answer_justification.fact: Statements 1 and 3 true; 2 false → option (c) 1 and 3 only.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Kill Statement 2 (any person can complain, not members only) → eliminate (a), (b), (d). Statements 1 (ad-hoc 2000→permanent 2015) and 3 (sub-judice bar) are straightforward.

concept_hooks: Lok Sabha Ethics Committee complaint procedure

850.trap_explanation: Statements 2 and 3 invert what Article 96(2) actually grants. The Speaker retains the right to speak AND to vote in the first instance during the removal debate — only tie-breaking is barred. UPSC exploits the intuition that someone facing removal should have no rights.

statements.text: He/She shall not preside.
statements.reason: Article 96(1): while a removal resolution is under consideration, the Speaker shall not preside even if present. The Deputy Speaker or another member chairs.

statements.text: He/She shall not have the right to speak.
statements.reason: Article 96(2) explicitly grants the Speaker the right to speak and otherwise take part in proceedings during consideration of the removal resolution.

statements.text: He/She shall not be entitled to vote on the resolution in the first instance.
statements.reason: Article 96(2) entitles the Speaker to vote in the first instance. The only restriction: no casting vote in case of equality of votes (tie-breaking is barred).

answer_justification.fact: Only Statement 1 is true; Statements 2 and 3 both contradict Article 96(2) → option (a) 1 only.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Article 96(2) is the pivot: it affirmatively grants right to speak AND vote in first instance. Statements 2 and 3 negate both → both false. Only S1 (no presiding, per Art. 96(1)) survives → (a).

concept_hooks: Speaker Lok Sabha casting vote Article 100

707.trap_explanation: The trap is doubting 'repeal' — aspirants assume amendment power covers only addition/modification. Article 368 explicitly includes repeal. All three modes are textually present in the article.

statements.text: Addition
statements.reason: Article 368(1) expressly empowers Parliament to amend the Constitution by way of addition.

statements.text: Variation
statements.reason: Article 368(1) expressly includes variation — i.e., modifying existing provisions.

statements.text: Repeal
statements.reason: Article 368(1) expressly includes repeal. All three modes are listed verbatim in the article.

answer_justification.fact: All three — addition, variation, repeal — are explicitly enumerated in Article 368(1). Answer: D.
answer_justification.elimination_path: If you recalled any one mode as valid, 'only 1 and 2' or 'only 2 and 3' options fall immediately. Article 368 text is exhaustive — all three.

708.trap_explanation: The trap is misremembering which Part covers which subject — especially conflating Part IX-A (municipalities) with Part IX (panchayats), or misplacing emergency provisions. All three statements are correct.

statements.text: Powers of the Municipalities are given in Part IX A of the Constitution.
statements.reason: Part IX-A (Articles 243P–243ZG), inserted by 74th Amendment 1992, covers municipalities. Part IX covers panchayats — common confusion.

statements.text: Emergency provisions are given in Part XVIII of the Constitution.
statements.reason: Part XVIII (Articles 352–360) covers National Emergency, President's Rule, and Financial Emergency.

statements.text: Provisions related to the amendment of the Constitution are given in Part XX of the Constitution.
statements.reason: Part XX contains only Article 368 — the amendment procedure. Single-article Part.

answer_justification.fact: All three Parts are correctly stated. Answer: D (1, 2 and 3).
answer_justification.elimination_path: Anchor on Part IX-A vs IX distinction to confirm statement 1. Part XVIII (emergency) and Part XX (amendment) are standard recall. All three hold.

709.trap_explanation: 'Inter-State' prefix makes options sound like they belong to states, not the Union. But inter-state subjects — trade, quarantine, migration — are Union List entries because they cross state lines and require central coordination.

answer_justification.fact: Inter-State quarantine is Union List Entry 81. The centre controls cross-border disease prevention.
answer_justification.hook: Anything 'inter-state' in List I: trade (Entry 42), migration (Entry 81 adjacency), quarantine (Entry 81).
answer_justification.elimination_path: A: Inter-State trade is Concurrent/Union, not State. B: Migration is Union List. D: Corporation tax is Union List Entry 85. Only C survives.

distractor_analysis.reason: Inter-State trade and commerce is Union List Entry 42, not a State subject.
Inter-State migration is Union List Entry 81, not State.
Corporation tax is Union List Entry 85 — exclusively central revenue.

concept_hooks: Union List State List Concurrent List entries

749.trap_explanation: Article 19 (freedom of speech, movement) feels like the natural home for privacy. Article 21's broader 'personal liberty' is the correct anchor per Puttaswamy 2017, but aspirants gravitate to 19.

answer_justification.fact: Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) — 9-judge bench unanimously placed Right to Privacy under Article 21 (right to life and personal liberty).
answer_justification.hook: Article 21 expanded by Maneka Gandhi (1978) to cover all personal liberty — Puttaswamy extended this to privacy.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Articles 15 and 16 are equality/non-discrimination — eliminate immediately. Between 19 and 21: Puttaswamy bench specifically anchored privacy in Article 21, not 19.

distractor_analysis.reason: Article 15 bars discrimination — unrelated to privacy.
Article 16 covers equality in public employment — not privacy.
Article 19 freedoms contributed to the reasoning but 21 is the primary anchor in Puttaswamy.
distractor_analysis.confused_with: Article 19(1)(a) freedom of speech — partial privacy overlap

826.trap_explanation: Statement 1 inverts the constitutional actor: it's the PRESIDENT (Article 342), not the Governor, who notifies STs. The Governor is only consulted. Statement 2 is true — ST lists are state-specific.

statements.text: It is the Governor of the State who recognizes and declares any community of that State as a Scheduled Tribe.
statements.reason: Article 342: President specifies STs by public notification, after consulting the Governor of that state. Parliament can modify by law. Governor only consulted, not the declaring authority.

statements.text: A community declared as a Scheduled Tribe in a State need not be so in another State.
statements.reason: ST notifications are state-specific — a tribe in Manipur may not appear on Assam's list. Lists vary by state via separate Presidential orders.

answer_justification.fact: Statement 1 false (President, not Governor, declares). Statement 2 true. Answer: B (2 only).
answer_justification.elimination_path: Article 342 recall kills statement 1 — Governor is only consulted. Once 1 is false, eliminate A and C. Statement 2 is straightforwardly true → B.

848.trap_explanation: Statement 4 is the trap: Rajya Sabha suggestions are NOT binding on Lok Sabha. Article 109(2) says Lok Sabha 'may' accept or not. Aspirants conflate 'suggestions' with 'amendments that must be accepted'.

statements.text: Article 109 mentions special procedure in respect of Money Bills.
statements.reason: Article 109 is titled and dedicated to the special procedure for Money Bills — textually correct.

statements.text: A Money Bill shall not be introduced in the Council of States.
statements.reason: Article 109(1): Money Bills are introduced only in Lok Sabha, never in Rajya Sabha.

statements.text: The Rajya Sabha can either approve the Bill or suggest changes but cannot reject it.
statements.reason: Article 109(2): Rajya Sabha can pass with/without amendments or make suggestions; it cannot reject. If not returned in 14 days, deemed passed.

statements.text: Amendments to a Money Bill suggested by the Rajya Sabha have to be accepted by the Lok Sabha.
statements.reason: Article 109(2): Lok Sabha 'may' accept or reject Rajya Sabha suggestions. Acceptance is discretionary, not mandatory.

answer_justification.fact: Statements 1, 2, 3 true; 4 false. Answer: C (1, 2 and 3).
answer_justification.elimination_path: Statement 4 kills options A and D. Between B and C: statements 1 and 3 are both correct (Article 109 scope + Rajya Sabha can't reject). Answer C.

concept_hooks: Money Bill vs Financial Bill distinction

851.trap_explanation: Statement 3 inverts the rule: a bill for which President has NOTIFIED joint sitting intent does NOT lapse on dissolution (Article 108 explicitly protects it). The opposite is stated — aspirants may assume all pending bills lapse.

statements.text: A bill pending in the Lok Sabha lapses on its dissolution.
statements.reason: Bills pending only in Lok Sabha (not yet passed by either house) lapse on dissolution — standard rule.

statements.text: A bill passed by the Lok Sabha and pending in the Rajya Sabha lapses on the dissolution of the Lok Sabha.
statements.reason: If Rajya Sabha hasn't yet passed it (and no joint sitting notification), the bill lapses with Lok Sabha dissolution.

statements.text: A bill in regard to which the President of India notified his/her intention to summon the Houses to a joint sitting lapses on the dissolution of the Lok Sabha.
statements.reason: Article 108 proviso: once President notifies joint sitting intent, the bill survives dissolution. Joint sitting can proceed even after Lok Sabha is dissolved.

answer_justification.fact: Statements 1 and 2 true; 3 false — Article 108 protects notified bills from lapsing. Answer: B (1 and 2).
answer_justification.elimination_path: Statement 3 is the pivot — Article 108 explicitly states joint-sitting-notified bill survives dissolution. Eliminate C and D. Statements 1 and 2 are standard lapse rules → B.

concept_hooks: Bill lapse Lok Sabha dissolution rules

852.trap_explanation: Statement 1 inverts the rule: prorogation also requires Council of Ministers advice (President acts on aid and advice per Article 74). Aspirants associate 'prorogation' as a purely Presidential/administrative act. Statements 2 and 3 are correct.

statements.text: Prorogation of a House by the President of India does not require the advice of the Council of Ministers.
statements.reason: Article 74 binds the President to act on Council of Ministers' advice for ALL executive functions including prorogation. No exception exists for prorogation.

statements.text: Prorogation of a House is generally done after the House is adjourned sine die but there is no bar to the President of India prorogating the House which is in session.
statements.reason: Convention: prorogation follows adjournment sine die. But constitutionally, the President can prorogue a House even while it is sitting — no textual bar.

statements.text: Dissolution of the Lok Sabha is done by the President of India who, save in exceptional circumstances, does so on the advice of the Council of Ministers.
statements.reason: Article 85(2): President dissolves Lok Sabha. Convention (Shamsher Singh 1974) binds this to Cabinet advice; President retains discretion only if PM loses majority.

answer_justification.fact: Statement 1 false; statements 2 and 3 true. Answer: C (2 and 3).
answer_justification.elimination_path: Article 74 kills statement 1 — Cabinet advice applies to prorogation too. Eliminate A and B. Statements 2 and 3 both hold → C.

concept_hooks: Article 74 aid and advice Council of Ministers

915.trap_explanation: Common meaning of 'prohibition' suggests banning a person or policy. Legal writ of Prohibition targets courts/tribunals — it tells a lower court to STOP proceedings, not government officers or legislatures.

answer_justification.fact: Writ of Prohibition: issued by superior courts (SC/HC) to lower courts/tribunals to halt proceedings exceeding jurisdiction — before a final order is passed.
answer_justification.hook: Prohibition = preventive; Certiorari = curative. Both target lower courts, not executive. Prohibition stops before; Certiorari quashes after.
answer_justification.elimination_path: A and D target government/officers — writs of Mandamus, not Prohibition. B involves legislatures — no writ applies this way. Only C (lower court, stop proceedings) fits.

distractor_analysis.reason: Mandamus directs government officers to perform duty; Prohibition targets courts.
No writ orders Parliament/Legislature to pass or refrain from legislation.
Government policy is challenged via Mandamus or Certiorari, not Prohibition.

concept_hooks: Writ of Prohibition vs Certiorari distinction

953.trap_explanation: Aspirants recall 2 or 3 Delimitation Commissions by memory. The question asks up to December 2023 — four formal Acts (1952, 1963, 1973, 2002) each created a Commission. No fifth was constituted by December 2023.

answer_justification.fact: Four Delimitation Commissions: 1952 (under Delimitation Commission Act 1952), 1963, 1973, 2002. No new commission by December 2023.
answer_justification.hook: Each major Delimitation Act created exactly one Commission. Four Acts = four Commissions.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Eliminate A (1) and B (2) — multiple commissions are documented. Eliminate C (3) — the 2002 commission is well-established as the fourth. Answer D.

distractor_analysis.reason: First commission was in 1952; multiple subsequent ones are a matter of record.
Two is an undercount — 1952, 1963, 1973, 2002 commissions all constituted.
Three undercounts — omits either 1952 or 2002 commission.

975.trap_explanation: Home Minister is ex-officio Chairman of NEC (post-2018 restructure), but the question asks about MEMBERS per Section 3 of the 2002 amended Act. Chairman ≠ member. Aspirants mark 4 (Home Minister) as a member because he chairs the body.

statements.text: Governor of the Constituent State
statements.reason: Section 3 of NEC Act (as amended 2002): Governors of the eight constituent NE states are members.

statements.text: Chief Minister of the Constituent State
statements.reason: Section 3: Chief Ministers of the eight constituent states are members of the NEC.

statements.text: Three Members to be nominated by the President of India
statements.reason: Section 3: Up to three members nominated by the President — added by 2002 amendment.

statements.text: The Home Minister of India
statements.reason: Home Minister is ex-officio Chairman (post-2018), not a statutory member under Section 3. Chairman and member are distinct roles under the Act.

answer_justification.fact: Members per Section 3: Governors, Chief Ministers, 3 Presidential nominees. Home Minister = Chairman, not member. Answer: A (1, 2 and 3 only).
answer_justification.elimination_path: Home Minister is ex-officio Chairman, not Section 3 member — kills options B, C, D. Items 1, 2, 3 are all Section 3 members → A.

1027.trap_explanation: Statement 1 inverts the timeline: implementation requires census + delimitation, targeting the 19th Lok Sabha (post-2029), not the 18th (already elected in 2024). The Act was passed during 18th LS — confusion between enactment and implementation.

statements.text: Provisions will come into effect from the 18th Lok Sabha.
statements.reason: Article 334A (inserted by 106th Amendment): reservation activates only after first post-commencement census and subsequent delimitation — applicable from 19th Lok Sabha at earliest.

statements.text: This will be in force for 15 years after becoming an Act.
statements.reason: Article 334A: reservation for women operative for 15 years from commencement, extendable by Parliament.

statements.text: There are provisions for the reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes Women within the quota reserved for the Scheduled Castes.
statements.reason: Act provides one-third of SC/ST reserved seats shall be reserved for SC/ST women respectively — sub-quota within existing SC/ST quota.

answer_justification.fact: Statement 1 false (19th LS, not 18th); 2 and 3 true. Answer: C (2 and 3 only).
answer_justification.elimination_path: Statement 1 fails on Article 334A — census+delimitation gate means 18th LS cannot implement. Eliminate A and B. Statements 2 and 3 are textually in the Act → C.

concept_hooks: 106th Constitutional Amendment Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam

1028.trap_explanation: Maithili is the distractor — it was added by the 92nd Amendment (2003), not the 71st (1992). UPSC tests whether aspirants conflate two different language-addition amendments.

statements.text: Konkani
statements.reason: 71st Amendment 1992 added Konkani to the Eighth Schedule, raising the total to 18 languages.

statements.text: Manipuri
statements.reason: 71st Amendment 1992 added Manipuri (also called Meitei) to the Eighth Schedule.

statements.text: Nepali
statements.reason: 71st Amendment 1992 added Nepali to the Eighth Schedule — all three added simultaneously.

statements.text: Maithili
statements.reason: Maithili was added by the 92nd Amendment 2003 (along with Bodo, Dogri, Santhali). Different amendment, different year.

answer_justification.fact: 71st Amendment (1992) added exactly Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali — three languages. Maithili came via 92nd Amendment 2003. Answer: A (1, 2 and 3).
answer_justification.elimination_path: Eliminate any option containing Maithili (4) — that's the 92nd Amendment 2003 intruder. Only option A (1, 2, 3) excludes Maithili.

1054.trap_explanation: Pairs 2 and 4 swap the leaders: C. Rajagopalachari founded the Swatantra Party (not Socialist Party); Acharya Narendra Dev was Socialist Party (not Swatantra). The correct leaders are cross-listed between the wrong parties.

pairs.reason: BJS founded 1951 by Shyama Prasad Mukherjee — unambiguous.
Rajagopalachari founded Swatantra Party (1959), not Socialist Party. Socialist Party: Acharya Narendra Dev, JP Narayan.
Congress for Democracy founded 1977 by Jagjivan Ram (with Bahuguna, Satpathy) after Emergency.
Swatantra Party (1959) was founded by C. Rajagopalachari. Narendra Dev was associated with Socialist Party.

answer_justification.fact: Pairs 1 and 3 correct; 2 and 4 wrong (Rajagopalachari and Narendra Dev swapped). Only two correct → Answer: B.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Pairs 2 and 4 are mirror-swapped errors. Rajagopalachari = Swatantra (not Socialist). Narendra Dev = Socialist (not Swatantra). Pairs 1, 3 solid → two correct → B.

concept_hooks: Bharatiya Jana Sangh Shyama Prasad Mukherjee
Congress for Democracy Jagjivan Ram 1977 Emergency

1092.trap_explanation: Storage and mineral exploration are the inversion traps. Storage of agricultural produce is tertiary (service: warehousing), not secondary. Mineral exploration is secondary (extraction), not tertiary. Dairy (production) is primary; weaving is secondary — both correct.

pairs.reason: Storage is a service (warehousing) → tertiary sector. No transformation of goods occurs.
Dairy farming = animal husbandry; production of raw material → primary sector.
Mineral extraction from nature → primary sector (not tertiary). Exploration is extraction-adjacent, still primary.
Weaving transforms raw yarn into cloth — manufacturing → secondary sector.

answer_justification.fact: Pairs 2 and 4 correct (dairy=primary, weaving=secondary); pairs 1 and 3 wrong → option (b) Only two.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Eliminate (d) immediately: pair 1 (storage=secondary) is wrong — storage is a service. Eliminate (c)/(a): pair 3 (mineral=tertiary) is wrong — extraction is primary. Pairs 2 and 4 correct → (b).

concept_hooks: Primary secondary tertiary sector India examples

1093.trap_explanation: Common sense says a plough 'does work' (feels active = working capital). Wrong. Fixed vs working capital = durable tool vs consumed-in-production input. Plough lasts years = fixed. Yarn/petrol are consumed in one cycle = working.

pairs.reason: Plough is durable; used repeatedly over years → fixed capital. Not consumed in one production cycle.
Computer lasts multiple years, not consumed in production → fixed capital. Correct per NCERT Class 10.
Yarn is entirely consumed in producing cloth → working capital, not fixed.
Petrol consumed in one use → working capital. Classic NCERT example.

answer_justification.fact: Pairs 2 and 4 correct (computer=fixed, petrol=working); pairs 1 and 3 wrong → option (b) Only two.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Key test: is the item consumed in one production cycle? Plough (no) → fixed, not working. Yarn (yes) → working, not fixed. Computer (no) → fixed ✓. Petrol (yes) → working ✓. Two correct → (b).

1094.trap_explanation: Both statements are true. The trap is doubting the explanatory link — students may think US not defaulting is a separate financial fact unconnected to 'full faith and credit.' But the absence of hard-asset backing IS precisely why a default makes bondholder claims unenforceable.

claim_statement.text: If the USA were to default on its debt, holders of US Treasury Bonds will not be able to exercise their claims to receive payment.
claim_statement.reason: US Treasuries are obligations backed only by the government's promise. Default = government refuses payment; no hard asset for bondholders to seize.

supporting_statements.text: The USA Government debt is not backed by any hard assets, but only by the faith of the Government.
supporting_statements.reason: True. US Treasuries carry 'full faith and credit' — no gold, property, or collateral. Default removes that faith, making bondholder claims unenforceable. Direct causal explanation.

answer_justification.fact: Both I and II true; II (no hard-asset backing) directly explains why default leaves bondholders with no recourse → option (a).
answer_justification.elimination_path: Verify I (default = no payment, true). Verify II (full faith and credit only, no hard assets — true). Does II explain I? Yes: fiat-only backing means default extinguishes all claims. → (a).

concept_hooks: US Treasury bonds full faith and credit

1268.trap_explanation: Both statements sound plausible but are false. WOS in India DO have a minimum paid-up capital of ₹500 crore. The RBI board rule is 'majority Indian nationals + at least one-third independent' — not a simple 50% threshold as stated in Statement 2.

statements.text: There is no minimum capital requirement for wholly owned banking subsidiaries in India.
statements.reason: RBI mandates minimum paid-up capital of ₹500 crore for foreign bank WOS in India. Statement directly contradicts this requirement.

statements.text: For wholly owned banking subsidiaries in India, at least 50% of the board members should be Indian nationals.
statements.reason: RBI requires majority of directors to be Indian nationals AND at least one-third to be independent directors — not a simple '50%' threshold as stated.

answer_justification.fact: Both statements false → option (d) neither 1 nor 2.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Statement 1: ₹500 crore minimum capital exists — kills (a) and (c). Statement 2: RBI rule is 'majority Indian + 1/3 independent,' not exactly '50%' — kills (b). → (d).

concept_hooks: RBI foreign bank subsidiary rules India
WOS wholly owned subsidiary banking RBI capital
Foreign bank board composition RBI guidelines

1269.trap_explanation: Statement I (risk spreading) is true and the defining feature of syndicated lending. Statement II falsely claims syndicated loans cannot be credit lines — they can be (revolving credit facilities are common). UPSC master was null; coaching consensus settles at (c).

claim_statement.text: Syndicated lending spreads the risk of borrower default across multiple lenders.
claim_statement.reason: Core feature of syndicated loans: a lead arranger brings in multiple banks, each taking a share, spreading default risk across the syndicate.

supporting_statements.text: The syndicated loan can be a fixed amount/lump sum of funds, but cannot be a credit line.
supporting_statements.reason: False. Syndicated loans routinely take the form of revolving credit facilities (credit lines). The 'cannot be a credit line' restriction does not exist.

answer_justification.fact: Statement I true (risk spreading confirmed); Statement II false (credit lines ARE possible in syndicated lending) → option (c).
answer_justification.elimination_path: Statement I: risk-spreading is the definition of syndicated lending — true. Statement II: revolving credit facilities exist in syndicated loans — 'cannot be credit line' is false. I correct, II wrong → (c).

1270.trap_explanation: Statement 3 is the kill: CBDC is NOT insured against inflation by design — it is a fiat currency subject to the same inflation risks as cash. Statements 1, 2, and 4 are all true. Confusing 'stable by design' with 'inflation-proof' is the trap.

statements.text: It is a sovereign currency issued by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) in alignment with its monetary policy.
statements.reason: Digital Rupee (e₹) is sovereign legal tender issued by RBI, integral to monetary policy. RBI Concept Note 2022 explicitly confirms this.

statements.text: It appears as a liability on the RBI's balance sheet.
statements.reason: Like physical currency, e₹ is an RBI liability. This is the defining feature distinguishing CBDC from commercial bank money.

statements.text: It is insured against inflation by its very design.
statements.reason: CBDC is fiat money — its value is not algorithmically fixed or commodity-backed. Inflation affects e₹ identically to physical cash.

statements.text: It is freely convertible against commercial bank money and cash.
statements.reason: e₹ is at par with cash; 1:1 convertibility with bank deposits and physical currency is a core design principle of India's CBDC.

answer_justification.fact: Statements 1, 2, 4 true; Statement 3 false (CBDC is not inflation-proof) → option (d) 1, 2 and 4.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Eliminate (b) and (c) first: both include statement 3 (inflation-insured) which is false for any fiat currency. Remaining options include (a) and (d); (d) adds statement 4 (convertibility, true) → (d).

1333.trap_explanation: CBLO sounds like a bond-market or stock-market instrument given the word 'Obligation.' It is a short-tenor, collateral-backed overnight/near-term instrument — squarely money market. CCIL operated it. Discontinued in 2018 (replaced by TREPS).

answer_justification.fact: CBLO = Collateralised Borrowing and Lending Obligation, operated by CCIL. Short-term, overnight to 1-year maturity → money market instrument.
answer_justification.hook: CCIL is the operator; the collateral is G-Secs/T-Bills. Same-day settlement makes it money market, not bond market.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Bond market (a): CBLO has no coupon, not tradable like bonds. Forex (b): no currency exchange involved. Stock market (d): not equity. Money market (c): short-term, collateral-backed overnight lending → correct.

distractor_analysis.reason: Bond market instruments are long-tenor coupon-bearing. CBLO is short-tenor collateral repo — no coupon.
Forex market involves currency exchange. CBLO is domestic rupee borrowing/lending.
Stock market = equity. CBLO involves no equity instruments; operates via G-Sec collateral.

1334.trap_explanation: Statement 1 is the kill-trap: NBFCs do NOT have access to RBI's LAF window — that is exclusively for scheduled commercial banks + primary dealers. FIIs can hold G-Secs (2); stock exchanges can offer debt platforms (3). Students who half-know NBFC regulatory access mark 1 as true.

statements.text: Non-Banking Financial Companies can access the Liquidity Adjustment Facility window of the Reserve Bank of India.
statements.reason: LAF (repo/reverse repo) is available only to scheduled commercial banks and primary dealers. NBFCs cannot borrow from RBI's LAF window.

statements.text: Foreign Institutional Investors can hold Government Securities (G-Secs).
statements.reason: FIIs/FPIs are permitted to invest in G-Secs under RBI's Foreign Portfolio Investment limits. Investment cap applies but access is permitted.

statements.text: Stock Exchanges can offer separate trading platforms for debts.
statements.reason: BSE and NSE both operate dedicated debt platforms. SEBI-regulated corporate bond trading is active.

answer_justification.fact: Statement 1 false (NBFCs excluded from LAF); 2 and 3 true → option (d) 2 and 3 only.
answer_justification.elimination_path: LAF exclusion of NBFCs kills statement 1 → eliminates (a) and (c). Statements 2 (FII G-Sec access ✓) and 3 (debt platform ✓) both true → option (d).

concept_hooks: Stock exchange debt trading platform India

1335.trap_explanation: The trap is assuming retail investors cannot trade corporate bonds or G-Secs — that they are institutional-only markets. RBI Retail Direct (2021) opened G-Sec access directly to individual retail investors. All three categories are permitted.

statements.text: Insurance Companies
statements.reason: IRDA mandates insurance companies hold G-Secs and corporate bonds as approved investments. They are major institutional participants.

statements.text: Pension Funds
statements.reason: PFRDA-regulated pension funds invest in both G-Secs and corporate bonds as per their investment mandate.

statements.text: Retail Investors
statements.reason: RBI Retail Direct Scheme (Nov 2021) allows individuals to directly buy G-Secs. SEBI also permits retail corporate bond trading on exchanges.

answer_justification.fact: All three — insurance, pension, and retail investors — can trade corporate bonds and G-Secs → option (d) 1, 2 and 3.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Anchor on retail: RBI Retail Direct (2021) demolished the 'retail can't buy G-Secs' assumption. Once retail (3) is confirmed, all three are in → eliminate (a), (b), (c) → (d).

concept_hooks: Insurance pension fund G-Sec investment India

1336.trap_explanation: Motor vehicles are real assets (tangible goods), not financial instruments. ETFs and currency swaps are financial instruments — one equity-based, one derivative. The trap is students unsure whether a currency swap qualifies as a 'financial instrument' and hedging to (a) only.

statements.text: Exchange-Traded Funds (ETF)
statements.reason: ETFs are securities traded on stock exchanges; they are standardised financial instruments representing a basket of assets.

statements.text: Motor vehicles
statements.reason: Motor vehicles are tangible physical assets — goods, not financial instruments. A financial instrument is a contract representing monetary value.

statements.text: Currency swap
statements.reason: Currency swaps are OTC derivative contracts — exchange of principal and interest in different currencies. Clearly a financial instrument.

answer_justification.fact: ETF and currency swap are financial instruments; motor vehicles are not → option (d) 1 and 3 only.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Kill motor vehicles (2) immediately — physical goods are never financial instruments. Eliminates (b) and (c). ETF (1) and currency swap (3) are both financial instruments → (d).

1373.trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the inversion trap: Companies Act 2013 Section 135 mandates 2% of average net profit for CSR — there IS a minimum spending requirement. Statement 1 (employee benefits excluded) is correctly stated. Marking 'both' or 'neither' are the likely wrong picks.

statements.text: Expenditures that benefit the company directly or its employees will not be considered as CSR activities.
statements.reason: Companies Act 2013 CSR rules explicitly exclude activities that benefit only employees or the company itself from the Schedule VII CSR definition.

statements.text: CSR rules do not specify minimum spending on CSR activities.
statements.reason: Section 135 mandates 2% of average net profit of preceding 3 years as minimum CSR spend for eligible companies. A floor clearly exists.

answer_justification.fact: Statement 1 true (employee benefit exclusion is explicit); Statement 2 false (2% net profit mandate exists) → option (a) 1 only.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Anchor on Section 135: 2% net profit minimum is foundational CSR law. Statement 2 says 'no minimum' — directly false. Eliminate (b), (c). Statement 1 (employee exclusion) is confirmed text of CSR rules → (a).

concept_hooks: CSR Schedule VII eligible activities India

1483.trap_explanation: Three distractors use common-sense definitions: births per 1000 people (birth rate), births per couple (not a standard measure), or birth-minus-death (natural growth rate). TFR is a woman-specific, lifetime average — a technical demographic concept distinct from all three.

answer_justification.fact: TFR = average number of live births a woman would have over her entire child-bearing period (ages 15-49). India's TFR ~2.0 per NFHS-5.
answer_justification.hook: TFR is per woman, not per couple, not per 1000 people. Child-bearing age = 15-49. Replacement TFR = 2.1.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Eliminate (a): births per 1000 = crude birth rate, not TFR. Eliminate (b): 'per couple' is not a demographic measure. Eliminate (c): birth rate minus death rate = natural growth rate. Only (d) matches the technical definition.

distractor_analysis.reason: Births per 1000 people = crude birth rate. TFR is per woman, not per population.
'Per couple' ignores single women and is not a standardised demographic indicator.
Birth rate minus death rate = natural rate of population growth, not TFR.

concept_hooks: TFR vs crude birth rate India

1526.trap_explanation: Statement 1 adds 'six months post-delivery' — PMSMA covers only antenatal care (2nd and 3rd trimester), NOT postnatal care. Statement 2 (voluntary private sector participation) is correctly stated. The postnatal insertion in S1 is the subtle fabrication.

statements.text: This scheme guarantees a minimum package of antenatal care services to women in their second and third trimesters of pregnancy and six months post-delivery health care service.
statements.reason: PMSMA covers antenatal care on the 9th of every month for 2nd/3rd trimester women only. No postnatal component exists under PMSMA.

statements.text: Under this scheme, private sector health care providers of certain specialities can volunteer to provide services at nearby government health facilities.
statements.reason: PMSMA explicitly invites private/NGO sector obstetricians, gynaecologists, and physicians to volunteer at government health facilities on the 9th of each month.

answer_justification.fact: Statement 1 false (no postnatal component); Statement 2 true (voluntary private sector participation) → option (b) 2 only.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Test S1 against PMSMA mandate: antenatal only, on 9th of month, 2nd/3rd trimester. 'Six months post-delivery' is a fabrication → eliminates (a) and (c). S2 (private volunteerism) is confirmed PMSMA design → (b).

1571.trap_explanation: Statement 1 says entry age 21-40; correct is 18-40. Statement 4 says family pension to 'spouse and unmarried daughters'; correct is 50% to spouse only. Statements 2 (age-specific contribution) and 3 (₹3000/month at 60) are correct. Multiple inversions in one question.

statements.text: The entry age group for enrolment in the scheme is 21 to 40 years.
statements.reason: PM-SYM entry age is 18-40 years, not 21-40. The lower bound of 18 is precise and commonly inverted in exams.

statements.text: Age specific contribution shall be made by the beneficiary.
statements.reason: PM-SYM uses age-based contribution slabs: younger entrants pay lower monthly premiums (₹55-₹200), which government matches 1:1.

statements.text: Each subscriber shall receive a minimum pension of ₹3,000 per month after attaining the age of 60 years.
statements.reason: Guaranteed minimum pension of ₹3,000/month at age 60 is the scheme's core promise, funded by beneficiary + Central Government contributions.

statements.text: Family pension is applicable to the spouse and unmarried daughters.
statements.reason: PM-SYM family pension = 50% of pension to spouse only upon subscriber's death. Unmarried daughters are not beneficiaries under the scheme.

answer_justification.fact: Statements 2 and 3 correct; Statements 1 (age=18 not 21) and 4 (spouse only, not daughters) false → option (b) 2 and 3 only.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Kill S1: entry age 18, not 21 → eliminates (a) and (d). Kill S4: family pension to spouse only, not daughters → eliminates (a) and (c). Survivors: S2 and S3 → (b).

concept_hooks: PM-SYM PM Shram Yogi Maandhan scheme

1590.trap_explanation: All three statements are true. The trap is doubting statement 1 (100% central funding sounds unusually generous) or statement 3 (transliteration sounds like a peripheral detail). DILRMP was restructured as 100% CSS in 2016; all three elements are confirmed programme components.

statements.text: To implement the scheme, the Central Government provides 100% funding.
statements.reason: DILRMP is a 100% Centrally Sponsored Scheme since its restructuring. States receive full central funding for land record digitisation components.

statements.text: Under the Scheme, Cadastral Maps are digitised.
statements.reason: Cadastral map digitisation is a core DILRMP component alongside computerisation of Records of Rights (RoR).

statements.text: An initiative has been undertaken to transliterate the Records of Rights from local language to any of the languages recognized by the Constitution of India.
statements.reason: DILRMP includes transliteration of RoR across Scheduled languages to enable inter-state portability and access. Active component of the programme.

answer_justification.fact: All three statements true → option (d) 1, 2 and 3.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Don't baulk at '100% central' — DILRMP is explicitly a 100% CSS (post-2016). Transliteration (S3) is an active DILRMP sub-component. All three confirmed → (d).

concept_hooks: Digital India Land Records Modernisation Programme

1677.trap_explanation: Both II and III are factually true AND both independently explain how rainfall weathers rocks — carbonic acid (II) causes carbonation, dissolved oxygen (III) causes oxidation. Students eliminate III thinking only CO2 matters for chemical weathering, picking (b) instead of (a).

claim_statement.text: Rainfall is one of the reasons for weathering of rocks.
claim_statement.reason: Rain drives chemical weathering via two distinct pathways: carbonic acid (carbonation) and dissolved oxygen (oxidation). Both dissolve and decompose minerals in rocks.

supporting_statements.text: Rain water contains carbon dioxide in solution.
supporting_statements.reason: CO2 + H2O → H2CO3 (carbonic acid). This acid dissolves limestone, feldspar, and other minerals — carbonation is a primary chemical weathering agent.
Dissolved O2 in rainwater oxidises iron-bearing minerals (e.g., pyrite → limonite/rust). Oxidation is a distinct, real chemical weathering pathway.

answer_justification.fact: Both II (carbonic acid) and III (oxygen-oxidation) are true AND both explain rainfall weathering → option (a).
answer_justification.elimination_path: Confirm II: rain absorbs CO2 → carbonic acid → carbonation (true, explains). Confirm III: dissolved O2 → oxidation of iron minerals (true, explains). Both explain → (a), not (b).

1678.trap_explanation: Students confidently include pyroclastic debris and ash but doubt nitrogen compounds — volcanoes are associated with SO2 and CO2, not nitrogen. However, volcanoes emit nitrogen compounds (N2, NOx) from magmatic gas and decomposed crustal material. All four are genuine volcanic products.

statements.text: Pyroclastic debris
statements.reason: Fragmented rock, lava, and ash ejected explosively. Core solid product of volcanic eruptions — unconditionally correct.

statements.text: Ash and dust
statements.reason: Fine pyroclastic material — volcanic ash is the most widely dispersed eruption product, reaching stratosphere and affecting climate.

statements.text: Nitrogen compounds
statements.reason: Volcanoes emit N2 (dominant atmospheric gas), ammonia, and NOx from magmatic degassing and thermal breakdown of country rock. Less publicised but confirmed.

statements.text: Sulphur compounds
statements.reason: SO2 is the signature volcanic gas; also H2S. SO2 → sulphate aerosols causing volcanic winter and acid rain. Classic eruption product.

answer_justification.fact: All four — pyroclastic debris, ash, nitrogen compounds, sulphur compounds — are genuine volcanic products → option (d) All four.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Pyroclastic + ash are certain (eliminate 'Only one'/'Only two'). Sulphur (SO2) is famous. Nitrogen compounds are the doubt-seed — but magmatic degassing produces N2 and NOx. All four confirmed → (d).

concept_hooks: Volcanic gases composition SO2 CO2 N2

1679.trap_explanation: June 21 is Northern Hemisphere summer solstice. Equator always gets exactly 12 hours — not more, not less. Tropic of Capricorn gets its shortest day (~10.5h). The trap inverts intuitions: Arctic Circle gets 24h, Tropic of Cancer gets ~13.5h. Equator and Capricorn are the eliminators.

statements.text: Equator
statements.reason: Equator receives exactly 12h of daylight every day of the year — sun rises due east and sets due west regardless of season.

statements.text: Tropic of Cancer
statements.reason: June 21 = Northern summer solstice. Sun is overhead at Tropic of Cancer — longest day ~13.5 hours. More than 12h confirmed.

statements.text: Tropic of Capricorn
statements.reason: June 21 is Southern Hemisphere winter solstice. Tropic of Capricorn has its shortest day (~10.5h) — well below 12h.

statements.text: Arctic Circle
statements.reason: Arctic Circle on June 21 experiences midnight sun — 24h of daylight. Far more than 12h.

answer_justification.fact: Tropic of Cancer (~13.5h) and Arctic Circle (24h) exceed 12h on June 21. Equator = exactly 12h, Capricorn = ~10.5h → option (d) 2 and 4.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Eliminate 1 (equator = perpetual 12h). Eliminate 3 (Capricorn = Southern winter, shortest day <12h). 2 and 4 remain → (d).

concept_hooks: Summer solstice June 21 day length latitude

1719.trap_explanation: Statement-I is factually wrong — the atmosphere is heated MORE by terrestrial (long-wave) radiation than by incoming solar (short-wave) radiation, which largely passes through. GHGs are transparent to short-wave but absorb long-wave. Most students mark I as true by intuition — the sun heats everything.

claim_statement.text: The atmosphere is heated more by incoming solar radiation than by terrestrial radiation.
claim_statement.reason: Solar short-wave radiation largely passes through the atmosphere (transparent to it). The atmosphere is mainly heated by terrestrial long-wave IR radiation absorbed by GHGs and clouds.

supporting_statements.text: Carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases in the atmosphere are good absorbers of long wave radiation.
supporting_statements.reason: True — GHGs absorb terrestrial IR radiation. But this supports why terrestrial radiation heats the atmosphere, directly contradicting Statement-I rather than explaining it.

answer_justification.fact: Statement-I is false (atmosphere heated by terrestrial long-wave, not solar short-wave). Statement-II is true → option (d).
answer_justification.elimination_path: Key inversion: solar radiation PASSES THROUGH atmosphere (short-wave, transparent). Terrestrial IR is ABSORBED by GHGs — that heats the atmosphere. I is the inverted statement. II is independently true → (d).

1720.trap_explanation: Both statements are true AND Statement-II genuinely explains Statement-I. The trap is marking (b) — assuming it's a coincidence rather than a causal chain. Convectional currents at the equator (driven by intense surface heating) physically push the tropopause higher.

claim_statement.text: Thickness of the troposphere at the equator is much greater as compared to poles.
claim_statement.reason: Troposphere is ~16-18 km at equator, ~8 km at poles. Heat-driven convection at equator raises the tropopause significantly higher.

supporting_statements.text: At the equator, heat is transported to great heights by strong convectional currents.
supporting_statements.reason: Intense solar heating at equator generates vigorous convection — warm air rises to great heights before cooling to lapse rate equilibrium, physically extending the troposphere upward.

answer_justification.fact: Both true; convectional currents directly cause the troposphere to extend higher at equator → option (a) II explains I.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Verify I (equator ~16-18 km, poles ~8 km — true). Verify II (convection driven by intense equatorial heating — true). Ask: does II cause I? Yes — convection physically lifts the tropopause. → (a).

1721.trap_explanation: Statement 2 inverts reality: water vapour is MAXIMUM in tropical regions (warm air holds more moisture), not at poles. Polar air is cold and dry — holds very little water vapour. Students may confuse 'ice and snow = water' with atmospheric water vapour content.

statements.text: It is a gas, the amount of which decreases with altitude.
statements.reason: Water vapour is concentrated in the lower troposphere (bulk in lowest 5 km). It decreases rapidly with altitude as temperature drops and air thins.

statements.text: Its percentage is maximum at the poles.
statements.reason: Water vapour is maximum in warm tropical regions — warm air has higher saturation capacity. Polar air is cold, dry, and holds minimal water vapour.

answer_justification.fact: Statement 1 true (decreases with altitude). Statement 2 false (maximum in tropics, not poles) → option (a) 1 only.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Statement 1 is basic thermodynamics — water vapour condenses as temperature falls with altitude. Statement 2 inverts the tropical-polar contrast. Poles are dry; tropics are humid → eliminate 2. Answer (a).

1722.trap_explanation: The description — low temperature range, year-round precipitation, 50-250 cm — fits Marine West Coast exactly. Equatorial climate has higher rainfall (>200 cm) and no winter. China-type and Humid Subtropical have hot summers and drier winters. The distractor pulls toward Equatorial since 'year-round rain' sounds tropical.

answer_justification.fact: Marine West Coast: mild winters, cool summers (low range), year-round rain heavier in winter, 50-250 cm total. Matches all three descriptors.
answer_justification.hook: Marine West Coast is the ONLY mid-latitude climate with year-round precipitation — all others have a dry season.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Equatorial: rainfall >200 cm, no winter, high temps. China-type/Humid Subtropical: hot humid summers, relatively dry winters. Marine West Coast: cool summers, mild winters, year-round rain → (d).

distractor_analysis.reason: Equatorial has high temperatures year-round, rainfall often >250 cm, no cool season — temperature range is NOT low in the mid-latitude sense.
China-type (Humid Subtropical) has hot, humid summers and mild winters — wider temperature range and less winter precipitation than Marine West Coast.
Humid subtropical has marked summer precipitation maximum and hot summers — not a low annual range or year-round uniform distribution.

1723.trap_explanation: Both statements about Coriolis force are correct. The trap targets Statement 1 — students often think Coriolis is purely latitude-dependent and forget velocity dependence. Coriolis force = 2mΩv·sinφ — both velocity (v) and latitude (sinφ) matter.

statements.text: It increases with increase in wind velocity.
statements.reason: Coriolis force F = 2mΩv·sinφ — directly proportional to velocity (v). Faster-moving air/objects experience stronger Coriolis deflection.

statements.text: It is maximum at the poles and is absent at the equator.
statements.reason: sinφ = 1 at poles (φ=90°), sinφ = 0 at equator (φ=0°). Maximum deflection at poles; zero deflection at equator — confirmed by the formula.

answer_justification.fact: Both statements correctly describe Coriolis force (F = 2mΩv·sinφ) → option (c) Both 1 and 2.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Apply F = 2mΩv·sinφ: Statement 1 — v appears (velocity proportional, true). Statement 2 — sinφ: max at pole, zero at equator (true). Both confirmed → (c).

1787.trap_explanation: Statement 1 is correct (January isotherms bow north over warmer oceans, south over colder continents in Northern Hemisphere). Statement 2 inversion: Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift are WARM currents, not cold. Their warmth bends isotherms poleward (north) — the mechanism is right but the current's thermal character is inverted.

statements.text: The isotherms deviate to the north over the ocean and to the south over the continent.
statements.reason: In January (Northern winter): oceans retain heat, isotherms deflect poleward (north). Continental land is cold; isotherms deflect equatorward (south). Classic ocean-continent isotherm pattern.

statements.text: The presence of cold ocean currents, Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift make the North Atlantic Ocean colder and the isotherms bend towards the north.
statements.reason: Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift are WARM currents. They warm the North Atlantic, pushing isotherms northward — the effect is right but they are labelled 'cold' (inversion).

answer_justification.fact: Statement 1 true (correct January isotherm pattern). Statement 2 false (Gulf Stream/NAD are warm, not cold currents) → option (a) 1 only.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Statement 2 trap: 'cold ocean currents, Gulf Stream' — Gulf Stream is definitively warm (originates in Gulf of Mexico). That one wrong word makes the whole statement false. Statement 1 is textbook correct → (a).

concept_hooks: January isotherms ocean continent Northern Hemisphere
Gulf Stream North Atlantic Drift warm current

1873.trap_explanation: UPSC tests the exact west-to-east sequence of Himalayan tributaries joining the Ganga after Prayagraj. The trap swaps Gomati and Ghaghara, and also shuffles Gandak-Kosi. Gomati joins first (near Ghazipur), then Ghaghara (Chhapra), Gandak (Hajipur), Kosi (Kursela).

answer_justification.fact: West-to-east sequence: Gomati (Ghazipur/UP) → Ghaghara (Chhapra/Bihar) → Gandak (Hajipur/Bihar) → Kosi (Kursela/Bihar) → option (b).
answer_justification.hook: Mnemonic: Go-Gha-Gan-Ko. Each river lies progressively east and north — Kosi is the easternmost, near the Nepal-Bihar border.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Eliminate (a): puts Ghaghara before Gomati — wrong. Eliminate (c) and (d): both place Kosi before Gandak — wrong (Gandak meets at Patna/Hajipur, Kosi much further east).

distractor_analysis.reason: Ghaghara before Gomati is reversed — Gomati joins at Ghazipur (west), Ghaghara at Chhapra (east of Ghazipur).
Kosi before Gandak is reversed — Gandak joins at Hajipur/Patna, Kosi joins further east at Kursela.
Both errors combined: Ghaghara before Gomati AND Kosi before Gandak — doubly wrong.

concept_hooks: Ganga tributaries sequence west east Bihar

1874.trap_explanation: Two of three pairs have geographic errors. Pair 1 misidentifies Dhuandhar's region as Malwa (it's near Jabalpur/Bhedaghat, not the Malwa plateau). Pair 3 misidentifies Gersoppa's river as Netravati (it's the Sharavati). Only Hundru-Subarnarekha-Chota Nagpur is correct.

pairs.reason: Dhuandhar falls are at Bhedaghat near Jabalpur (Mahakoshal/Satpura region), NOT Malwa plateau. River (Narmada) is correct; region is wrong.
Hundru Falls on the Subarnarekha River near Ranchi, Jharkhand — in the Chota Nagpur plateau. All three elements correct.
Gersoppa (Jog Falls) is on the Sharavati River in Shimoga/Sagar district, Karnataka — NOT the Netravati. Region (Western Ghats) is correct; river is wrong.

answer_justification.fact: Only Pair 2 (Hundru-Subarnarekha-Chota Nagpur) is fully correct → option (a) Only one.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Confirm Pair 2 first (Hundru on Subarnarekha, Ranchi — unambiguous). Pair 1: region 'Malwa' is wrong (Jabalpur not Malwa). Pair 3: Gersoppa = Sharavati, not Netravati. Two wrong, one right → (a).

concept_hooks: Jog Falls Gersoppa Sharavati River Karnataka

1993.trap_explanation: The question asks specifically about Greenfield airports — built on virgin land from scratch. Vijayawada airport is an existing airport that has been upgraded and expanded, NOT built as a Greenfield project. Donyi Polo (2022) and Kushinagar (2021) are the genuine Greenfield constructions.

statements.text: Donyi Polo Airport
statements.reason: Donyi Polo Airport, Itanagar — inaugurated November 2022. First airport in Arunachal Pradesh; built as a Greenfield project on previously undeveloped land.

statements.text: Kushinagar International Airport
statements.reason: Kushinagar International Airport inaugurated October 2021 as a Greenfield project to serve Buddhist pilgrimage circuit in eastern UP.

statements.text: Vijayawada International Airport
statements.reason: Vijayawada airport (Gannavaram) is an existing airport. It has received upgrades but was NOT constructed as a Greenfield project.

answer_justification.fact: Donyi Polo (Arunachal, 2022) and Kushinagar (UP, 2021) are confirmed Greenfield. Vijayawada is an upgraded legacy airport → option (a) 1 and 2 only.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Eliminate 3 (Vijayawada = Gannavaram, pre-existing airport). Confirm 1 (first airport of Arunachal Pradesh, entirely new). Confirm 2 (Buddhist circuit, new construction 2021) → (a).

concept_hooks: Donyi Polo Airport Arunachal Pradesh first airport

2036.trap_explanation: All four options are African countries — the trap exploits vague Africa-cocoa association without specificity. Algeria and Morocco are North African (Mediterranean), Botswana and Namibia are southern arid-belt. Cocoa is a humid tropical crop; the correct pair (Côte d'Ivoire + Ghana) lies in West Africa's equatorial zone.

answer_justification.fact: Côte d'Ivoire (~40%) and Ghana (~20%) together produce ~60% of world cocoa — first and second globally by volume.
answer_justification.hook: Both are on the Gulf of Guinea in West Africa — the world's cocoa belt. If one African option has two adjacent coastal West African countries, that's your answer.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Eliminate (a): Algeria + Morocco = North Africa, arid/Mediterranean — no cocoa. Eliminate (b): Botswana + Namibia = southern arid — no cocoa belt. Eliminate (d): Madagascar + Mozambique = East Africa, not major cocoa. Only (c) is West Africa's humid equatorial zone.

distractor_analysis.reason: Algeria and Morocco are North African, semi-arid to arid. No significant cocoa cultivation — wrong climate zone entirely.
Botswana (landlocked, arid Kalahari) and Namibia (Namib Desert) — dry savanna/desert climates, unsuitable for cocoa.
Madagascar and Mozambique are East African — minor cocoa producers far behind Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana.

concept_hooks: Côte d'Ivoire Ghana cocoa world production

2037.trap_explanation: Pair 1 has two errors: Vosges is in Europe (France-Germany border), not Central Asia, and it's a block/horst mountain not a fold mountain. Pair 2 inverts Alps and block: Alps are young fold mountains, not block. Pairs 3 and 4 are correct.

pairs.reason: Vosges are in northeast France (Alsace), NOT Central Asia. And they are block/horst mountains (fault-bounded), not fold mountains — double error.
Alps are in Europe (correct region) but are classic young FOLD mountains formed by Alpine orogeny — not block mountains. Type is wrong.
Appalachians are old fold mountains in eastern North America — correct on all three: region, name, type.
Andes are young fold mountains along western South America, formed by subduction of Nazca Plate — correct on all three.

answer_justification.fact: Pairs 3 (Appalachians, old fold) and 4 (Andes, young fold) correct; pairs 1 and 2 wrong → option (b) Only two.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Pair 1: 'Central Asia' is wrong (Vosges = France). Pair 2: 'Block mountain' is wrong (Alps = young fold). Pairs 3 and 4 are textbook correct. Two correct → (b).

concept_hooks: Mountain types fold block volcanic UPSC

2074.trap_explanation: Finland borders the Gulf of Bothnia and Baltic Sea — not the North Sea. Russia's western coasts touch the Baltic Sea and Barents Sea — the North Sea border stops at Norway. Only Germany and Norway (of the four listed) actually border the North Sea, making the answer 'Only two'.

statements.text: Finland
statements.reason: Finland's coastline is on the Gulf of Bothnia and Baltic Sea. It has no border with the North Sea — separated by Norway and Sweden.

statements.text: Germany
statements.reason: Germany has a North Sea coastline in the states of Schleswig-Holstein and Lower Saxony — confirmed North Sea border.

statements.text: Norway
statements.reason: Norway's entire western coastline faces the North Sea — one of its primary maritime boundaries.

statements.text: Russia
statements.reason: Russia borders the Barents Sea (north), Baltic Sea (Kaliningrad enclave) — not the North Sea. The North Sea does not reach Russian territory.

answer_justification.fact: Only Germany and Norway (of the four) border the North Sea → option (b) Only two.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Eliminate Finland (Baltic/Gulf of Bothnia). Eliminate Russia (Barents Sea/Baltic — not North Sea). Germany and Norway confirmed. Two countries → (b).

concept_hooks: Finland coastline Baltic vs North Sea

2075.trap_explanation: Russia-Kazakhstan or China-India feel long because they conjure vast continental imagery. The Canada-USA border (~8,891 km including the Alaska segment) is the world's longest, but test-takers associate 'big borders' with Russia's land mass or the China-India dispute. The answer is counterintuitively the North American pair.

answer_justification.fact: Canada-USA border is ~8,891 km (including Alaska-Canada boundary) — the longest international border between any two countries.
answer_justification.hook: Russia-Kazakhstan is second (~7,644 km). Canada-USA beats it because the Alaska boundary adds ~2,475 km of separate US-Canada border segment.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Eliminate (c) China-India (~3,488 km, disputed). Eliminate (b) Chile-Argentina (~5,308 km). Eliminate (d) Kazakhstan-Russia (~7,644 km — second longest). Only (a) Canada-USA at ~8,891 km wins.

distractor_analysis.reason: Chile-Argentina border ~5,308 km (Andes spine) — long but well below Canada-USA.
China-India border ~3,488 km (disputed LAC) — not even close to the longest.
Kazakhstan-Russia border ~7,644 km — second longest globally, but Canada-USA (~8,891 km) exceeds it.

concept_hooks: Canada USA international border length Alaska

2076.trap_explanation: Both statements are correct and less intuitively obvious. Students may doubt statement 2 (expecting some river to drain into the Red Sea) or statement 1 (assuming surrounding countries have some rainfall). The Red Sea is flanked by the Arabian and Saharan deserts — almost no rain, and no major river drains into it.

statements.text: The Red Sea receives very little precipitation in any form.
statements.reason: Red Sea is surrounded by hyper-arid regions (Arabian Desert, Sahara). Annual rainfall over the Red Sea is extremely low — among lowest globally for any sea body.

statements.text: No water enters the Red Sea from rivers.
statements.reason: No major river drains into the Red Sea. The Nile drains to Mediterranean; Arabian Peninsula rivers are ephemeral wadis that don't reach the Red Sea consistently. No freshwater dilution occurs.

answer_justification.fact: Both true: minimal precipitation AND no river inflow → high evaporation produces ~40 psu salinity. Option (c) Both 1 and 2.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Statement 1: Red Sea = surrounded by desert — minimal rain (true). Statement 2: Nile drains to Mediterranean; no perennial river reaches Red Sea (true). Both confirmed → (c).

concept_hooks: Red Sea salinity high evaporation no rivers
Arabian Desert Sahara Red Sea climate

2120.trap_explanation: Centipedes and termites are not parasitoids — centipedes are predators, termites are detritivores. Carabid beetles (some), flies (Tachinidae), and wasps (Ichneumonidae, Braconidae) all have parasitoid species. Students conflate 'deadly to hosts' with 'parasitoid lifestyle'.

statements.text: Carabid beetles
statements.reason: Some carabid (ground beetle) larvae are parasitoids on soil-dwelling insects. Not all are — but parasitoid species exist within Carabidae.

statements.text: Centipedes
statements.reason: Centipedes are active predators, not parasitoids. They kill hosts immediately — parasitoids by definition develop in/on a living host before killing it.

statements.text: Flies
statements.reason: Tachinidae flies are entirely parasitoid — larvae develop inside arthropod hosts, eventually killing them. One of the largest parasitoid families.

statements.text: Termites
statements.reason: Termites are eusocial detritivores (wood/cellulose feeders). No parasitoid behaviour — they do not lay eggs in/on hosts.

statements.text: Wasps
statements.reason: Ichneumonidae and Braconidae wasps are the most species-rich parasitoid group. Females inject eggs into caterpillars, aphids, spiders — larvae consume host from within.

answer_justification.fact: Carabid beetles, flies, wasps = three. Centipedes (predators) and termites (detritivores) are not parasitoids → option (b).
answer_justification.elimination_path: Reject centipedes (active predators, kill immediately) and termites (detritivores). Wasps and flies are textbook parasitoids; carabid beetles have parasitoid species → three → (b).

2121.trap_explanation: Groundnut looks like a cereal or oilseed, and horse-gram looks like a food grain — both tempt students to place them outside Fabaceae. All three are legumes: they fix nitrogen, have compound leaves and pods, and belong to family Fabaceae (Leguminosae).

statements.text: Groundnut
statements.reason: Arachis hypogaea — family Fabaceae. Geocarpic legume; pods ripen underground but it is a true pea-family member with nitrogen-fixing nodules.

statements.text: Horse-gram
statements.reason: Macrotyloma uniflorum — family Fabaceae. A drought-hardy legume grown across peninsular India; classic pulse crop.

statements.text: Soybean
statements.reason: Glycine max — family Fabaceae. Highest-protein legume crop globally; nitrogen-fixing.

answer_justification.fact: All three — groundnut, horse-gram, soybean — are Fabaceae (Leguminosae) → option (c).
answer_justification.elimination_path: Anchor on the nitrogen-fixing pod criterion: all three have pods and root nodules. None are cereals (grass family). All three → (c).

2122.trap_explanation: Froghopper (spittlebug) sounds amphibian — students may pick reptiles or fish. Pond skater lives on water — suggesting fish. All three are true insects (Order Hemiptera), distinguished by piercing-sucking mouthparts.

answer_justification.fact: Cicada (Cicadidae), froghopper (Cercopidae), pond skater (Gerridae) — all Order Hemiptera, class Insecta.
answer_justification.hook: Froghopper's name is deceptive — it jumps like a frog but is a bug. Pond skater walks on water but breathes air — insect.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Eliminate birds (no wings mentioned, wrong body plan). Eliminate fish and reptiles (all three are terrestrial/surface arthropods). Hemiptera are insects → (c).

distractor_analysis.reason: Birds are vertebrates with feathers. None of these organisms are avian — all are invertebrate arthropods.
Fish are aquatic vertebrates. Pond skater lives on water surface but is an insect — it does not have gills or fins.
Reptiles are vertebrates with scales. Froghopper's name misleads — it is not an amphibian or reptile.

2123.trap_explanation: All three pairs scramble correct country-animal assignments. Indri is native to Madagascar (not Brazil). Elk is native to Eurasia and North America — not Indonesia. Bonobo is native to DR Congo (not Madagascar). None of the three pairs are correct.

pairs.reason: Indri (Indri indri) is endemic to the rainforests of northeastern Madagascar — not found in Brazil or anywhere outside Madagascar.
Elk (Cervus canadensis) is native to North America and East Asia; Cervus elaphus ranges Europe to Central Asia. Indonesia has no wild elk population.
Bonobo (Pan paniscus) is endemic to the Congo Basin, Democratic Republic of Congo — south of the Congo River. Madagascar has no great apes.

answer_justification.fact: Indri → Madagascar; Bonobo → DR Congo; Elk → Eurasia/North America. All three pairs are wrong → option (d) None.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Indri is Madagascar-only — pair 1 (Brazil) is wrong. Bonobo is Congo-only — pair 3 (Madagascar) is wrong. Elk is not found in Indonesia — pair 2 is wrong. All three fail → (d).

2124.trap_explanation: Statement 3 is the planted inversion: leopards DO scent-mark their territories, just like lions. The question says they do NOT — which is false. Statements 1 (lions breed year-round) and 2 (cheetahs cannot roar — lack the modified hyoid bone) are both correct.

statements.text: Lions do not have a particular breeding season
statements.reason: Lions are non-seasonal breeders — they mate and give birth year-round, unlike many temperate mammals with defined rut periods.

statements.text: Unlike most other big cats, cheetahs do not roar
statements.reason: Cheetahs lack the two-part modified hyoid apparatus that enables lions, tigers, leopards, and jaguars to roar. They chirp, purr, and yelp instead.

statements.text: Unlike male lions, male leopards do not proclaim their territory by scent marking
statements.reason: Leopards extensively scent-mark with urine, faeces, and claw marks on trees — identical territorial signalling to lions. Statement reverses the fact.

answer_justification.fact: Statements 1 and 2 true; Statement 3 false (leopards do scent-mark) → option (a) 1 and 2 only.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Kill Statement 3 first — leopards are well-known scent markers. That eliminates options (b) and (d). Both 1 (year-round breeding) and 2 (no roar = no hyoid modification) are factual → (a).

2125.trap_explanation: Sandalwood and mahua have famous insect associations (lac insect, honey bees) — students may pick them. But only fig trees have an obligate, exclusive co-evolved relationship with Agaonidae fig wasps: each fig species is pollinated by one unique wasp species.

answer_justification.fact: Fig (Ficus spp.) and Agaonidae fig wasps: strictly mutualistic, co-evolved obligate partnership. Each Ficus species has one wasp pollinator species that can enter its enclosed syconium.
answer_justification.hook: The fig is not a fruit but an enclosed inflorescence (syconium) — only the species-specific fig wasp can enter and pollinate it.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Mahua attracts bees and bats but is not exclusive to one. Sandalwood is hemiparasitic, not exclusively insect-pollinated. Silk cotton has wind and bat pollination. Only fig has a described, exclusive wasp co-evolution → (a).

distractor_analysis.reason: Mahua (Madhuca longifolia) attracts generalist pollinators — bees, beetles, birds. No exclusive co-evolved insect pollinator.
Sandalwood (Santalum album) is hemiparasitic; pollinated by various insects. No exclusive single-species pollinator relationship.
Silk cotton (Bombax ceiba) is pollinated by bats and birds primarily — not an exclusive insect co-evolution.

2126.trap_explanation: Students doubt whether butterflies are truly 'poisonous' — poison usually means harmful when touched/eaten (not injected). Monarch butterflies sequester cardenolides from milkweed; poison dart frogs sequester alkaloids; pufferfish contain tetrodotoxin. All three groups have documented toxic species.

statements.text: Butterflies
statements.reason: Monarch butterfly (Danaus plexippus) sequesters toxic cardenolides from milkweed — birds that eat monarchs vomit. Several other Danainae are similarly toxic.

statements.text: Fish
statements.reason: Pufferfish (Tetraodontidae) contain tetrodotoxin, one of the most potent neurotoxins. Stonefish have venomous spines. Multiple fish species are poisonous or venomous.

statements.text: Frogs
statements.reason: Poison dart frogs (Dendrobatidae, South America) sequester alkaloids from diet — skin contact or ingestion is toxic. Some species are among the most toxic vertebrates.

answer_justification.fact: All three groups — butterflies, fish, frogs — have well-documented poisonous species → option (c).
answer_justification.elimination_path: Don't doubt butterflies — Monarch's cardenolide toxicity is documented. Fish (pufferfish tetrodotoxin) and frogs (poison dart) are textbook. All three → (c).

2162.trap_explanation: Cashew and papaya are both widely cultivated in India and feel 'Indian' — but both were introduced from the Americas by Portuguese traders. Only red sanders (Pterocarpus santalinus) is truly native, endemic to the Eastern Ghats of Andhra Pradesh.

statements.reason: Anacardium occidentale — native to northeastern Brazil. Portuguese brought it to Goa in the 16th century as a soil stabiliser, then spread it across India.

statements.text: Papaya
statements.reason: Carica papaya — native to southern Mexico and Central America. Introduced to India via Portuguese and Spanish traders in the 16th-17th century.

statements.text: Red sanders
statements.reason: Pterocarpus santalinus — endemic to the Eastern Ghats (mainly Andhra Pradesh). Listed in CITES Appendix II; IUCN Endangered. Genuinely native and ecologically restricted to this zone.

answer_justification.fact: Only red sanders is native to India. Cashew and papaya are both South/Central American introductions → option (a) Only one.
answer_justification.elimination_path: Cashew = Brazil origin (Portuguese to Goa, ~1560). Papaya = Central America (Portuguese introduction). Red sanders = Eastern Ghats endemic, CITES-listed. Only red sanders survives → (a).

2242.trap_explanation: Both statements are true AND Statement II directly explains Statement I — plastic gum base (polyisobutylene, polyvinyl acetate) is the specific reason chewing gum is an environmental pollutant. Unlike natural chicle-based gum, synthetic gum base does not biodegrade.

claim_statement.text: Many chewing gums found in the market are considered a source of environmental pollution.
claim_statement.reason: Chewing gum is the second most-littered item globally (after cigarette butts). The synthetic base is non-biodegradable and accumulates on pavements.

supporting_statements.text: Many chewing gums contain plastic as gum base.
supporting_statements.reason: True. Modern gum bases use polyisobutylene and polyvinyl acetate — both synthetic polymers (plastics). This is precisely why gum does not biodegrade and pollutes.

answer_justification.fact: Both I and II true; II (plastic gum base) directly explains I (pollution source) → option (a).
answer_justification.elimination_path: Verify II: polyisobutylene = synthetic rubber polymer = plastic. That substance makes gum non-biodegradable. Direct causal link to pollution → both true, II explains I → (a).
